function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

Below is a practical “recipe” you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your CI/CD pipeline).  
I’ll walk through each numbered step, show the exact shell commands you’d run, and supply the content for the three files you need to generate.

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually clone, edit, or push the repository for you.  
> The commands below assume you’re working on a machine that already has `git`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and `jq` installed, and that you have SSH access to the GitHub repo (`git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`).  

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1.1 Make sure you’re in the directory where you want the repo
cd ~/projects   # change this to whatever makes sense for you

# 1.2 Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you already have a local copy, just `cd nodejs-welcome` and skip the `git clone`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Detect the dominant language

We’ll use a quick `jq`‑based script that counts the number of lines per language in the repo.  
(If you prefer, you can also use `linguist` or `cloc`.)

```bash
# 2.1.1 Install cloc if you don’t have it
sudo apt-get install -y cloc   # Debian/Ubuntu
# brew install cloc           # macOS

# 2.1.2 Run cloc and parse the output
LANGUAGE=$(cloc --json . | jq -r '.languages | to_entries[] | select(.value.code > 0) | "\(.key):\(.value.code)"' | sort -k2nr | head -n1 | cut -d':' -f1)

echo "Dominant language detected: $LANGUAGE"
```

> **Result** – For this repo you’ll see something like `JavaScript`.  
> If you get a different result, adjust the subsequent templates accordingly.

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Create a minimal Dockerfile that uses the detected language’s runtime.  
For JavaScript (Node.js) we’ll use an official Node image.

```bash
cat <<'EOF' > Dockerfile
# 2.2.1 Base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# 2.2.2 Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# 2.2.3 Copy package.json and lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# 2.2.4 Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# 2.2.5 Copy the rest of the source
COPY . .

# 2.2.6 Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# 2.2.7 Default command
CMD ["npm", "start"]
EOF
```

> **Why `node:18-alpine`?**  
> Alpine images are small and fast. Adjust the version if your app requires a specific Node LTS release.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a single file `k8s/deployment.yaml` that contains both Deployment and Service objects.

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
cat <<'EOF' > k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
EOF
```

> **Notes**  
> * `replicas: 3` – you can tweak this.  
> * `image:` – replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual registry you’ll push to.  
> * `service.type: LoadBalancer` – if you’re on a cloud provider that supports LB, otherwise use `ClusterIP` or `NodePort`.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Add a workflow that builds the Docker image, pushes it to GitHub Container Registry, and optionally applies the K8s manifests.

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat <<'EOF' > .github/workflows/build-and-deploy.yml
name: Build & Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: k8s/deployment.yaml
        images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}   # optional: only if you want to auto‑deploy
EOF
```

> **What this does**  
> * Builds the image on every push to `main`.  
> * Pushes it to GitHub Container Registry under `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
> * Optionally deploys to a cluster if you provide a `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` secret.  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication – no extra secrets needed for the build step.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-deploy.yml
```

If you want to stage everything that changed:

```bash
git add .
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on a protected branch that requires PR reviews, you’ll need to open a pull request instead of pushing directly.

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, verify that the workflow ran:

1. Go to **Actions** tab → find the latest run → click it.  
2. Confirm that the “Build and push Docker image” step succeeded.  
3. If you enabled the deploy step, check your cluster (`kubectl get pods,svc`) to see the new resources.

---

## Recap

| Step | What you did |
|------|--------------|
| 1 | Cloned the repo locally |
| 2.1 | Determined dominant language (JavaScript) |
| 2.2 | Created a Dockerfile that installs deps and starts the app |
| 2.3 | Generated a Deployment + Service YAML for Kubernetes |
| 2.4 | Added a GitHub Actions workflow that builds/pushes the image |
| 3 | Staged the new files |
| 4 | Committed and pushed to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image registry, or service type to fit your environment. Happy coding!
